doc.title: Sam Most interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 15, 1999

title: Rock and roll gigs he could not do
summary: He quit a band that became eighty percent rock and roll because he would not memorize record riffs.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Yeah. Well it’s never been the most popular kind of music. Have you ever had occasion where people ask you to do something in the rock & roll vein?

I’ve had to play a few gigs before. I was playing with one group that at first it was only ten percent rock & roll, then it came to be eighty percent rock & roll so I didn’t stay with the band but you had to play certain things like they had these disco things or else the saxophone player had to play [scats]. I don’t mean, I’m not singing it right but [scats] or certain, on the groove. And so I had to learn the phrases on the record like [scats], that type of thing. And I couldn’t remember anything anyhow so all those things that you had to play rock & roll. So after a while I says I didn’t fit in because I couldn’t play the riffs that were on the record. I never wanted to memorize them. I was trying to memorize Charlie Parker solos.

So as I say when it became like eighty percent that, “I Get No Satisfaction” and I can’t remember all the titles of the things like, you know I can’t remember some of the tunes so then I didn’t work with those groups.
